items.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: a Music Minus One record with Clark Terry and a rhythm section.

ctx.x: Well, I think that’s fantastic. What happens is that... A lot of us will play with records, and of course, the melody and everything is already there, so you’re trying to mimic what’s there, which is not a bad thing. But now you have this incredible rhythm section that’s laying the foundation there, plus, then, the duration of time that one piece is played from beginning to end gives the student the opportunity to do a lot of exploration, versus it being very short and truncated. It’s hard to develop those ideas…

It sure was. Yeah, you’ve got me copied exactly. Yes. As a matter of fact, and I’ve probably still got it somewhere here, a Music Minus One record with Clark Terry and a rhythm section. We played the melody, he’d solo a chorus or two, then he’d stop and you solo a chorus or two. I bought that record. I was thinking, “boy, I wish he’d stop playing; I’ve got Clark Terry on records; I don’t need to hear him play.” Just give me 4 or 5 minutes of just the rhythm section. That’s why I did what I did. And after I did…
There you’ve got Volume 6 with Charlie Parker, and then Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins and Woody Shaw.

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He jumped up and said, “What had this got to do with jazz education, all these jokes that people are telling?”

ctx.x: Jamey Abersold. He jumped up and said, “What had this got to do with jazz education, all these jokes that people are telling?” I was 100% in favor of what he had said. A lot of the effort – the time is wasted in the wrong direction. I think they could do a far better job.
[The recording resumes on a new topic after a change of tape.]
